content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket.

The employee is Jesus Cooke (E029), requesting write access to Source Code.

Two notes from team memory:
- Note 1 (HR?): role Payroll Specialist, employment type full_time, recommendation write.
- Note 2 (Security?): role Payroll Specialist (not looked up in own database, same value), employment type contractor (looked up in own database), security training basic, recommendation read.

Conflict: employment type is either full_time (note 1) or contractor (note 2). Note 2 explicitly says Security DB shows contractor with basic security training, and notes it's not full-time as previously noted. Note 2 was "looked up in own database" for employment type, while note 1 also says looked up in own database. Hmm, conflicting.

Access policy:
- full_time: up to write. Admin only if role owns system. Payroll Specialist doesn't own Source Code (Engineer owns Source Code). So full-time max is write.
- contractor: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin. This contractor has basic training, so max is read.

Requested: write.

If full-time: write is allowed → grant write.
If contractor with basic training: max is read → grant read.

The question is which note to trust. The Security agent looked up employment type in their own database (the security DB) and found contractor with basic training. Note 1's employment type "full_time" was also looked up in own database. But note 2 explicitly corrects: "Security DB shows Jesus Cooke (E029) is a contractor with basic security training (not full-time as previously noted)."

As the approver, I should weigh the evidence. The Security note explicitly flagged the discrepancy and provided their DB lookup showing contractor. This seems like a more specific/corrected fact.

Given the contractor status with basic training, max is read. Requested write exceeds maximum, so grant read.

I'll submit read.
